strengths: The paper presents an original and potentially useful interpretability paradigm: functionally localize word-responsive units in vision-language models, intervene on them, and evaluate the resulting behavioral dissociations.

The main Qwen2-VL result is intuitively interesting: targeted ablation substantially reduces held-out lexical-decision accuracy while performance on the selected visual-reasoning tasks is largely preserved.

The study includes several valuable controls and analyses, including random-unit ablation, perturbation magnitude, different layer types, phonological versus orthographic stimulus sets, and preliminary experiments on additional model families.
The manuscript is clearly organized and visually polished, and it explains the motivation, methodology, and qualitative failure modes accessibly.
The use of neuroscience-derived localizer stimuli and human behavioral tests offers a promising bridge between mechanistic model analysis and cognitive-science hypotheses.
weaknesses: The central interpretation is substantially stronger than the evidence. Units selected by contrasting images of words against faces, objects, and scrambled words may simply support OCR, lexical recognition, or general text-in-image processing. No neural-response alignment, spatial/topographic correspondence, representational analysis, or sufficiently demanding controls with letters, false fonts, numerals, and matched nonwords establish that these distributed language-decoder units are an analogue of the human VWFA.

The intervention demonstrates that units selected for word responsiveness are important for a word-recognition task, which is partly expected by construction. Moreover, the layer type and mask size are selected according to the desired ROAR-versus-RAVEN behavior, while the same benchmark-level dissociation is then treated as confirmatory evidence. Holding out ROAR items does not remove this benchmark and analysis-selection circularity.

The statistical analysis is not convincing. Twenty resampled localizer masks are compared against a single intact-model baseline using one-sample Student t-tests. These seeds are not independent model or participant samples, task items are not treated as the sampling unit, and uncertainty in the baseline is ignored. Consequently, the very small p-values and confidence intervals likely reflect pseudoreplication rather than robust inferential evidence. Multiple testing is also not addressed.

The claimed dyslexia threshold is poorly justified for model accuracy. Human ROAR assessment incorporates psychometric calibration and response speed, whereas the model experiment uses accuracy alone; directly assigning a 65% clinical threshold to the model is not validated. The mask is then explicitly enlarged until it crosses this constructed threshold, making crossing it weak evidence for dyslexia.

The non-reading controls are too limited to establish preserved general ability: RAVEN contains only 12 easy items, Kempler sample size is not reported, and several intact scores are at ceiling. Kempler also supplies language through text tokens rather than the image-reading pathway being lesioned. Broader OCR, object recognition, visual-language, semantic, and text-only controls are needed, along with importance- and activation-matched ablations.

Ablation removes a very large fraction of decoder MLP units (about 6.89%) and sometimes produces blank, corrupted, or incoherent output. These failures resemble generic model damage rather than a specific human reading disorder. Random ablation is not an adequate control because randomly chosen units can differ greatly in activation scale and causal importance from the selected units.

The phonological conclusion is unsupported. The model receives no auditory information, and reduced accuracy on visually presented homophones or pseudohomophones does not by itself isolate phonological computation. The two stimulus categories may differ in baseline difficulty, lexicality, item count, or ceiling effects. The model also fails to reproduce the significant orthographic deficit in the cited human data, so the claimed human-like profile is incomplete.

Evidence of generality is weak. LLaVA-NeXT performs below chance on the reasoning control, and PixTral uses only five seeds, has a low RAVEN baseline and wide uncertainty, and lacks the full set of random/importance-matched controls. Thus only the principal, post-selected model provides the complete reported dissociation.

Essential reproducibility details are missing or insufficiently explicit, including localizer and benchmark sample sizes, stimulus splits for all tasks, prompts, decoding settings, precise unit definition and intervention hooks, scoring rules for malformed responses, and per-item results. An anonymized code link is helpful but does not replace these details in the paper.

The discussion's language about digital twins, causal neural mechanisms, biomarkers, interventions, and dyslexia-friendly fonts is clinically and scientifically premature. The work supports an analogy involving model components, not conclusions about the causal biology of developmental dyslexia, and it does not adequately address the risks of anthropomorphizing model lesions or translating them into clinical claims.

strengths: The paper poses an interesting interdisciplinary question and presents an intuitive localization–ablation–behavior framework for studying reading-related computation in vision-language models.
The evaluation includes held-out ROAR items, random-unit ablations, layer and perturbation analyses, two additional model architectures, and comparisons across reading and non-reading tasks.
The authors examine phonological and orthographic conditions separately and acknowledge that the model reproduces only part of the human behavioral profile.
The manuscript is generally readable, with useful diagrams and qualitative examples of post-ablation behavior.
weaknesses: The central brain-model analogy is not established. Units selected by contrasting word images against faces, objects, and scrambled images could simply be generic text/OCR-sensitive units; there is no neural-response alignment, anatomical correspondence, or control using visually matched pseudowords or other letter strings to justify calling them an artificial VWFA.

The experiment is partly circular: the ablation size is explicitly increased until ROAR performance crosses a chosen dyslexia threshold, after which crossing that threshold is presented as evidence that dyslexia has been induced. Holding out items from the same task distribution does not eliminate this construct-level selection bias.

The 65% human diagnostic threshold is transferred directly to model accuracy without showing that human and model score distributions are commensurable. Dyslexia is also a developmental, heterogeneous disorder, whereas the intervention zeros roughly 6.89% of distributed language-MLP units in a pretrained model.

Evidence that non-reading abilities are preserved is weak. Raven contains only 12 items, Kempler appears to be a small binary VQA task, and failure to obtain a significant decrease is treated as evidence of equivalence. Broader OCR, language, vision, and reasoning benchmarks are absent, despite qualitative outputs showing blank or corrupted generations indicative of general damage.

The statistical analysis is not convincing. Twenty resampled localizer masks are treated as independent observations and compared against a single intact-model score using one-sample t-tests; item uncertainty, benchmark size, mask-selection bias, and multiple testing are not adequately handled. Vague reports such as p ≪ 0.01 further limit auditability.

The random-unit control is insufficiently matched. Random units are not demonstrably matched for activation magnitude, variance, layer position, or general causal importance. Stronger controls would include text-selective but non-lexical units, object-selective units, high-activation units, and masks optimized for comparable overall output degradation.

The claimed human correspondence is incomplete and overstated: human participants exhibit significant orthographic impairment in the cited comparison, while the model does not. Grouping heterogeneous lexical-decision conditions into broad 'phonological' and 'orthographic' scores also requires considerably more justification, sample details, and item-level analysis.

Cross-model generalization remains limited. LLaVA is uninterpretable because its Raven baseline is below chance, while PixTral provides only a narrow comparison with high uncertainty and lacks the full set of random, layer, and behavioral controls used for the main model.

Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are missing, including localizer sample counts, activation pooling/token selection, precise unit definitions, prompts and decoding settings, benchmark sizes beyond ROAR and Raven, and complete raw per-condition results.

The discussion substantially exceeds the evidence by describing these systems as digital twins and suggesting implications for biomarkers, interventions, and dyslexia-friendly fonts. The paper does not adequately address the ethical and conceptual risks of equating destructive model ablations with a human neurodevelopmental condition.

strengths: Creative and well-motivated framework combining neuroscience-inspired functional localization with causal ablation in vision-language models.

The central result is compelling: ablating word-selective language-MLP units disproportionately harms lexical decisions while selected visual-reasoning and sentence-grounding capabilities remain comparatively preserved.

Useful controls and analyses include held-out ROAR items, matched random-unit ablations, perturbation-strength and layer-type studies, phonological-versus-orthographic tests, and experiments on additional VLMs.

The phonological analysis provides a more specific behavioral signature than a generic OCR-performance decline, and the paper appropriately acknowledges that the human orthographic deficit is not reproduced.
The manuscript is clearly written, visually polished, and relevant to both mechanistic interpretability and computational cognitive neuroscience.
weaknesses: The biological claims exceed the evidence. Causally relevant OCR units in a VLM are not necessarily an analogue of the human VWFA, and the experiments do not validate a causal account of developmental dyslexia, a digital twin, or proposed clinical interventions. There is no neural-alignment evidence, developmental modeling, patient-level prediction, or anatomical/topographic correspondence.

The statistical design is problematic. The 20 observations are localizer resamples evaluated on the same test items and compared against one fixed intact-model score; treating them as independent observations in one-sample t-tests risks pseudoreplication. Uncertainty should be estimated over both localizer samples and benchmark items using paired, hierarchical, or bootstrap analyses.

Evidence that general abilities remain intact is narrow. RAVEN uses only 12 easy items, the Kempler and diagnostic-test sample sizes are insufficiently documented, and two control tasks cannot establish preserved general visual intelligence or language comprehension. Cross-model support is also limited because LLaVA-NeXT is at chance on RAVEN and PixTral has substantial uncertainty.

Some methodological choices are outcome-driven: the mask size is chosen to cross the ROAR threshold, and the language-MLP layer type is favored because it produces the desired selectivity. A fully nested validation procedure is needed to separate model and hyperparameter selection from confirmatory evaluation.

The 65% human-derived dyslexia threshold is not convincingly transferable to a VLM. The model is evaluated without response time and is not calibrated onto the human ROAR scale, so crossing this cutoff should not be interpreted as diagnosing or quantitatively reproducing dyslexia.

Blank, gibberish, and corrupted responses after ablation raise the possibility that some ROAR degradation reflects generation instability rather than a selective reading impairment. Output-validity rates and controls involving OCR transcription, text-only lexical decisions, ordinary VQA, and matched nonword visual stimuli would help distinguish these explanations.

Important reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including exact localizer sample counts and resampling, prompts and decoding settings, several benchmark sample sizes, ablation implementation, raw per-item predictions, and treatment of multiple comparisons. Overall, the paper is promising and marginally above threshold, but its conclusions should be narrowed and the evaluation strengthened.

strengths: The manuscript presents a creative, potentially useful localization-ablation framework connecting mechanistic VLM analysis with cognitive neuroscience, and the motivation and experimental narrative are unusually clear. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/8a10232466e942a581d691233dc7b35c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The use of neuroscience-derived word-versus-control localizers is principled, and targeted ablation produces a striking dissociation between lexical-decision performance and the reported nonverbal benchmarks.

The paper includes several useful controls and extensions: matched-count random ablations, perturbation-strength and layer-type analyses, evaluation on two additional VLMs, phonological versus orthographic stimuli, and an initial comparison with human fMRI responses.
The presentation is accessible, figures are generally clear, exact task prompts are provided, and the authors expose qualitative failure modes rather than reporting only aggregate accuracy.
weaknesses: The central interpretation substantially exceeds the evidence. Ablating word-responsive units in an artificial language decoder and impairing visual lexical decisions demonstrates a model subnetwork for reading, but does not by itself constitute a mechanistic model of developmental dyslexia. The selected units are distributed across all 80 decoder blocks rather than forming an analogue of a localized cortical area, and biological development, connectivity, learning history, and subject heterogeneity are absent.

The main selectivity claim lacks adequate controls. RAVEN contains only 12 easy items and Kempler uses a text prompt, while the observed ROAR failures include blank, corrupted, and incoherent generations. Thus, the results may reflect task-conditional language-generation or OCR failure rather than dyslexia-like reading errors. Stronger controls should include visual OCR transcription, text-only lexical decisions, general image-text tasks, broader language generation, and ablations matched for activation magnitude or causal impact rather than merely unit count.

The experimental choices are partly outcome-selected: the ablation size is explicitly chosen to cross the proposed dyslexia threshold, and the MLP layer type is selected because it yields the desired ROAR/RAVEN dissociation. Although ROAR has a held-out split, the broader layer, mask-size, and benchmark selection procedure risks circularity and is not validated on an independently specified confirmatory suite.

The 65% 'dyslexia threshold' is not validly transferred from humans to VLM accuracy. The paper does not provide the underlying human ROAR mean and variance supporting this exact cutoff, and prevalence statistics do not establish comparability between human norm scores and model item accuracy. Crossing this tuned threshold therefore cannot diagnose a dyslexia-like state.

The statistical analysis is weak. Localizer resampling seeds are treated as independent observations while item and subject uncertainty is largely ignored; a fixed intact baseline is tested with one-sample, one-tailed t-tests; numerous masks, layers, tasks, fonts, and subset sizes are compared without correction; and sample sizes are missing for Kempler, the Luke et al. subsets, localizer categories, and fMRI subjects/voxels. RAVEN's 12 items make claims of preserved reasoning especially underpowered.

The neural-alignment evidence is incomplete and not clearly VWFA-specific. Critical dataset and preprocessing details are absent, significance is assessed across five resampled masks rather than human subjects, no comparison with other cortical regions is given, and random units equal or outperform selected units beyond roughly 1.25%. Small encoding-score differences therefore provide limited validation of a human VWFA analogue.

The human behavioral correspondence is selective and partly contradictory: the model fails to reproduce the significant orthographic deficit observed in the cited human dataset, whose paper is itself framed as evidence for an orthographic rather than phonological deficit. Calling the model human-like or supportive of the dominant causal account requires more careful treatment of competing dyslexia theories.

The font experiment is presented as a human prediction without quantitative human validation. Font categories rely on heterogeneous recommendations and personal reports, rendering parameters are only approximately controlled, and size, spacing, stroke, and background color are confounded. Generic OCR robustness could explain the pattern.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the stated code availability: the manuscript omits the number and sampling of localizer stimuli, activation token/spatial aggregation, exact unit definition, generation and decoding settings, ablation-hook implementation, model precision, full per-model mask sizes and results, and detailed fMRI encoding choices.

Claims about digital twins, diagnosis, biomarkers, other psychiatric conditions, and intervention/font design are premature. The paper also lacks a substantive limitations and ethics discussion addressing anthropomorphism, stigmatizing simulations of neurodivergence, and risks of deriving clinical recommendations from VLM behavior. Overall, the empirical phenomenon is interesting, but major conceptual, statistical, and validation gaps keep the work below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The localization–ablation–behavior framework is an interesting and potentially useful connection between mechanistic interpretability and cognitive neuroscience.

The paper includes several sensible experimental components: held-out ROAR items, random-unit ablations, non-reading control tasks, layer and perturbation analyses, replication on two additional VLMs, and a preliminary comparison with human fMRI responses.
The central qualitative result is clear: units selected for responsiveness to visual words affect image-based lexical decisions more than the reported visual-reasoning controls.
The manuscript is generally readable, well illustrated, and unusually transparent about prompts and examples of corrupted model outputs.
weaknesses: The central biological interpretation is not justified. The selected units are distributed across MLP gate projections in all 80 language-decoder blocks, and roughly 6.89% of those units are completely zeroed. This is neither anatomically analogous to a focal VWFA nor physiologically analogous to VWFA hypoactivation. It primarily establishes an artificial subnetwork important for OCR-like lexical decisions, not a computational model of developmental dyslexia.

The experimental procedure is substantially outcome-driven. The mask size is explicitly increased until ROAR crosses a hand-chosen “dyslexia threshold,” and the language MLP component is selected because it gives the desired task dissociation. A held-out ROAR subset helps, but does not address selection among layer types, mask sizes, perturbation strengths, tasks, and interpretations. Independent confirmatory evaluation is needed.

The 65% threshold is not convincingly calibrated. Human ROAR assessment involves more than raw accuracy, including response-time information, while the paper neither reports the human mean and variance used to obtain 65% nor demonstrates that VLM accuracy is commensurate with human clinical scores. Crossing this threshold therefore does not establish dyslexia-like behavior.

The controls are too weak to demonstrate selective preservation of general abilities. RAVEN contains only 12 easy items and appears subject to coarse measurement and ceiling effects; Kempler is another small, narrow VQA task. Missing controls include ordinary OCR, text recognition, spelling, visual classification, broader language generation, and matched nonword/character tasks. Blank, gibberish, and corrupted outputs after ablation are evidence of broader model damage that accuracy on these two controls cannot exclude.

The statistical analysis likely overstates certainty. Twenty resampled localizer masks applied to the same model and benchmark items are treated as independent observations, while the intact baseline is fixed. This does not capture item, model, or participant variability. One-tailed tests, extensive testing across masks, layers, tasks, and fonts, and no stated multiple-comparison correction make the very small p-values difficult to interpret.

The claim that the model mirrors human phonological dyslexia is contradicted by the presented human data: humans show significant phonological and orthographic impairments, whereas the ablated model shows only the former. The cited Luke et al. study is explicitly positioned around an orthographic rather than phonological account, yet the manuscript dismisses the mismatch speculatively using unavailable comorbidity metadata. Moreover, a model with no auditory input performing visual lexical decisions provides limited evidence about phonological mechanisms.

The fMRI analysis is under-specified and weak as biological validation. Essential details such as subject and voxel counts, stimulus construction, activation pooling, ridge regularization, and uncertainty across subjects are absent. The reported advantage over random units is small, uses only five resampled masks, disappears at 2.5%, and reverses at larger subset sizes. Random units are also an insufficient comparison to standard visual, OCR, or language representations.

The font experiment does not validate human-like font sensitivity: it compares results against informal recommendations and personal reports rather than matched human measurements. Font size is only kept “as similar as possible,” multiple tests are uncorrected, and the literature supporting special dyslexia fonts is not critically discussed. Claims about predicting interventions or designing beneficial fonts are therefore unsupported.

Replication on Molmo and Pixtral is limited to ROAR and the 12-item RAVEN test, with five masks and no random-ablation controls, neural validation, or detailed deficit characterization. It does not establish that the proposed mechanism generalizes.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated code availability: the manuscript omits localizer sample counts, precise unit-activation definitions and token/spatial aggregation, decoding and scoring settings, several benchmark sample sizes, complete numerical results, and important fMRI preprocessing details.

The clinical and causal rhetoric is substantially stronger than the evidence. Terms such as “digital twins,” claims about causal neural mechanisms, biomarkers, screening, interventions, and generalization to psychiatric disorders are inappropriate for a behaviorally tuned lesion of an artificial network. The paper provides no meaningful limitations or ethics discussion addressing stigmatization, medical validity, or risks of extrapolating VLM behavior to neurodevelopmental conditions.

strengths: The paper presents a creative and potentially impactful idea: using functional localization and targeted ablation in vision-language models to study selective cognitive impairments. The localization-ablation-behavior framework is intuitive, clearly motivated, and well presented. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/74566127d074402e833e8d3a194a847c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The principal empirical dissociation is interesting: ablating word-selective units substantially reduces lexical-decision performance while leaving the reported Raven and Kempler scores largely intact. Matching random-unit ablations by layer and number is a useful control.

The study evaluates several dimensions beyond the primary lexical-decision benchmark, including phonological and orthographic stimuli, human fMRI prediction, fonts, and replication on Molmo and Pixtral. This breadth makes the work more substantial than a single-model lesion demonstration.
The manuscript is engaging, visually polished, and unusually accessible for interdisciplinary work spanning interpretability, vision-language modeling, and cognitive neuroscience.
weaknesses: The statistical analysis treats different resamplings of a fixed localizer set as independent experimental observations. These runs use the same model and largely overlapping evaluation items, so one-sample t-tests over seeds substantially overstate the effective sample size. Item-level uncertainty, subject-level uncertainty for the neural analysis, correction for multiple comparisons, and direct interaction tests for claimed dissociations are missing. This undermines many reported significance claims.

There are important researcher-degrees-of-freedom and potential circularity concerns. The mask size is explicitly selected to push ROAR performance below a predefined threshold, and the language-MLP component is emphasized because it produces the desired selective pattern. Although the final ROAR items are held out, stronger validation would require freezing all localization, layer, mask-size, and threshold decisions before evaluation on independent tasks and models.

The evidence establishes a task-selective lesion in a VLM, but not a mechanistic model of developmental dyslexia. Ablation frequently produces blank, incoherent, or corrupted generations, suggesting disruption of output generation rather than a clean reading impairment. Controls for OCR, visual word transcription, general lexical knowledge, non-reading generation quality, and matched task/output formats are needed.

The human comparison is weak. Model and human results come from different experimental settings, response time—central to reading fluency—is omitted, and the model does not reproduce the significant human orthographic impairment. Calling its visual lexical-decision errors a phonological deficit is especially difficult to justify without auditory representations or a formal model-by-group interaction.

The fMRI result is under-specified: the number of subjects and voxels is not reported in the analysis, five resampled masks are used as the apparent uncertainty unit, and random subsets differ from ranked word-selective subsets in feature correlation and representation. The observed encoding advantage therefore does not securely identify an artificial analogue of the VWFA.

The font experiment is presented as a prediction of human dyslexia-friendly typography, but it lacks direct human validation, relies partly on recommendations and personal reports, and performs many comparisons without an evident multiplicity correction. Font size, glyph geometry, image rendering, and background changes are also potential confounds.

Evaluation of preserved general ability is narrow: Raven contains only 12 easy items and Kempler is a small, format-different VQA task. The claimed generality to other models is relegated to a brief appendix with only five seeds and limited numerical or methodological detail.

Several conclusions—such as describing the model as a digital twin, inferring causal mechanisms of dyslexia, supporting screening biomarkers, and informing interventions—are substantially stronger than the evidence. The framing also risks conflating a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition with destructive unit ablation; the paper needs a clearer limitations and responsible-use discussion.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite including prompts: essential details about localizer sample counts, activation/token aggregation, decoding and scoring, image construction, benchmark sizes, mask selection granularity, and the full neural-analysis protocol are absent or insufficiently specified. Overall, the idea is promising and the empirical pattern merits follow-up, but the current statistical and construct-validity problems are too substantial for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
